reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a front-running bot as a way to earn substantial passive income by having viewers deploy and fund a contract with Ether. It describes profiting by inserting a higher-gas transaction ahead of a pending victim's transaction and reports returns of four or more Ether per week, while acknowledging that results are not always profitable. The records do not establish whether the contract worked as described or whether viewers lost funds.

Well guys, I want to share the profit bot made for me. So I have something around 1.26 Ether, which is around 25%.
Sometimes it's not always profitable, but usually I make four plus Ethereum a week.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present returns as certain. He says, "Sometimes it's not always profitable," and the description warns that a poorly funded contract could "waste your money in fees rather than using it to make profit." Those qualifications matter when assessing whether this is a deceptive promise, rather than a risky trading demonstration. The account of four-plus Ether a week is framed as his usual experience, not as an assured result for every viewer. The available material does not establish that the stated returns occurred, but it also does not establish that the speaker concealed the possibility of losses.

citations.quote: Sometimes it's not always profitable, but usually I make four plus Ethereum a week.
If you fund the contract with less than 1 ETH, the bot might target another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste your money in fees rather than using it to make profit.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies funding instructions and reported profits, but those facts alone do not show a guaranteed return or prove that the contract failed to trade. It also quotes the speaker's admission that results are not always profitable. His explanation of transaction ordering describes the proposed trading method; the record does not verify the method's effectiveness or establish that viewers lost their deposits.

citations.quote: Sometimes it's not always profitable, but usually I make four plus Ethereum a week.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A risk qualification does not undo the central pitch. The description recommends funding the contract with around 1 to 10 ETH, while the speaker links putting in more Ether to making more profit. He then reports rapid gains and says he usually makes four-plus Ethereum a week. Whether those results were real is unverified, but the video still encourages viewers to fund a purported profit-generating bot.

opening.argument: The video's substance is a walkthrough of a Solidity workflow. The speaker directs viewers to create a contract file, match the compiler version to the code, select a deployment environment, and confirm deployment. The sampled screen shows the Remix IDE and its deployment interface. Funding and starting the contract are presented as subsequent steps in that walkthrough, while the claimed earnings are the speaker's account of what happened afterward. A tutorial can include an asserted use case without the supplied evidence proving either that the code works or that its author intends to take viewers' funds.

Now under Compiler, we are going to select our version to 0.6.6 so it matches our contract.
Here we need to select Injected Web 3 as the environment.
Well guys, I want to share the profit bot made for me.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening treats instructions to fund and start the contract as decisive. But those instructions sit within a step-by-step account of creating, compiling, deploying, and operating it. The profit figures are reported as the speaker's experience; the cited transcript does not independently verify them or show that a viewer's funds were diverted. The tutorial framing remains relevant even though the proposed application is speculative.

citations.quote: Now we need to click on the compileBot.sol button and wait for the file to compile.
So the next step here is to click start.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The interface walkthrough is the means by which viewers are directed to fund the purported bot. The speaker says more funding will produce more profit, instructs viewers to send Ether to the contract, and presents a roughly 40% gain after about a day. Showing compilation and deployment does not substantiate that the contract can deliver those returns or turn the funding pitch into merely neutral programming instruction.

So it basically took me about a day to gain my deposit by more than a third,. Something close to 40%, which isn't that bad.

opening.argument: This is presented as operating a contract deployed through the viewer's connected wallet, not as paying the speaker for access to an investment service. The speaker instructs viewers to check the contract address, send Ether to that address, and use a withdrawal action described as returning funds to their wallet. Those are claims about the workflow, not proof that withdrawal actually works; equally, the supplied material does not show the speaker receiving deposits or requesting credentials. The described profit is conditional on trading activity and fees, rather than an explicit guaranteed payout. On this record, a risky purported trading tool is a narrower reading than a demonstrated scheme to take viewers' money.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution is right that viewers are told to fund a contract. But its opening does not establish who controls that contract's funds or whether its withdrawal function works. The speaker describes deploying to a connected wallet and later withdrawing to that wallet. Those assertions deserve scrutiny, not automatic acceptance; the same evidentiary restraint applies to inferring diversion of funds from the funding step alone.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Proof that the speaker personally receives deposits is not required to assess the pitch. Viewers are directed to copy supplied code, deploy it, and fund the resulting contract; the description recommends around 1 to 10 ETH. The claim that withdrawal returns principal and profit is the speaker's assertion, not verification of the contract's behavior. The purported trading mechanism and substantial earnings claims remain central regardless of whether the video asks for credentials.
